title: Mine — Area Overview (mining sequence)
model_title: Bauxite Mine — Area Overview (mining sequence from clearing to rehabilitation)

introduction.definition: This area model shows the whole open-cut bauxite mining sequence on one lateritic plateau. Read the model from right to left to follow one block through time: forest, clearing, stripping, drill and blast, ore mining to the clay floor, backfill and rehabilitation. The mining face itself advances to the right, into the forest, and rehabilitation follows behind it on the left. Trucks run the load–haul–dump cycle in real time from the excavators to the primary sizing station. The scene uses a thin (~4 m) ore column and short hauls for clarity; thicker ore (up to 10–30 m on East Coast India-type deposits) is mined in several flitches or benches, and real hauls are 2–8 km. Tap any machine to open its detailed model.
applications: Understanding the mining sequence and where each machine works
Seeing the lateritic profile on the cut face: topsoil, overburden, caprock, bauxite, clay
Following the ore from the face to the sizing station and ROM pad
key_points: Plateau bauxite is flat-lying and shallow: strip mining with a low strip ratio (~0.3–0.6 t waste per t ore, estimate)
Caprock (ferricrete) is drilled and blasted, and mined as ore or waste depending on its grade. The ore below is mostly free-digging or ripped; occasional hard bands are blasted

Grade control (available Al₂O₃, reactive SiO₂) decides what is ore and which grade bin it goes to. Available Al₂O₃ = gibbsite alumina extractable in a low-temperature (~145 °C) caustic digest; reactive SiO₂ = kaolinite silica that consumes caustic as DSP

Caprock is classified by grade-control assay: where available Al₂O₃ and reactive SiO₂ meet the ore cut-off it goes to the sizer as ore, otherwise to backfill as waste (reference plant: ~50 % assumed ore, to be confirmed)
Topsoil is kept separate and returned quickly — the seed bank is the key to rehabilitation
Clearing-to-rehabilitation takes ~1–3 years per pit (progressive rehabilitation); rehabilitated pits are left as shallow depressions because the ore removed is not replaced

classification.type: Open-cut plateau bauxite mine (strip mining with progressive rehabilitation)

introduction.summary: The bauxite mine area model shows the whole mining sequence on one plateau, from undisturbed forest on the right to rehabilitated land on the left: clearing, topsoil and overburden stripping, caprock drill-and-blast, excavation of the ore down to the kaolinitic clay floor, backfill, and rehabilitation. The cut face shows the lateritic profile: topsoil, laterite overburden, ferricrete caprock, friable gibbsitic bauxite and clay. Trucks run the real-time load–haul–dump cycle from the excavators, up the 10 % box-cut ramp and along the haul road to the primary sizing station; the ROM pad holds the grade-bin blending reserve.

what_to_look_for: The front edge of the block is a cut face that shows the lateritic profile: topsoil (~0.25 m), overburden (~1 m), ferricrete caprock (~1.5 m), gibbsitic bauxite (~4 m here, undulating base) and the kaolinitic clay floor.

steps.text: 0 · Grade control: RC/aircore drilling on a ~7.5–15 m grid with 0.5–1 m samples is assayed for available Al₂O₃ and reactive SiO₂; ore/waste and grade-bin polygons are loaded into excavator GPS guidance and the fleet-management system.
1 · Clearing: timber salvaged, vegetation mulched — as late as possible before mining.
2 · Stripping: topsoil (seed bank) and overburden removed separately by dozers and loaders.

3 · Caprock drill & blast: the drill rig works a pegged ~3.0 × 3.5 m pattern (burden × spacing) set by the blast design, tighter in thin caprock, working toward the free face; the blast breaks the cemented ferricrete into muck.

4 · Load & haul: the blasted caprock is loaded out first (to the sizer if grade control classes it as ore, otherwise to backfill); the ore is then dug in one or two flitches down to the clay floor. The ore excavators stand on the exposed ore surface and top-load trucks waiting on the floor below, swinging to the side of the body, never over the cab.
5 · Trucks climb the 10 % ramp and run the haul road to the primary sizing station, reverse square to the wheel stop and tip (at a ROM-pad finger: tip short of the crest and let the dozer push).
6 · Backfill and rehabilitation: landform reshaped, topsoil returned, deep ripped on the contour and replanted.

The front edge of the block is a cut face that shows the lateritic profile: topsoil (~0.25 m), overburden (~1 m), ferricrete caprock (~1.5 m), gibbsitic bauxite (~4 m here, undulating base) and the kaolinitic clay floor.

working_principle.characteristic_curve: Mine schedule: tonnes of ore per year at the target available alumina and reactive silica, blended through grade bins and the ROM pad.

mine_planning: Resource drilling (~60–120 m grid) and grade-control drilling (~7.5–15 m grid) define ore pods and grade bins.
Pit sequence planned so clearing, mining and rehabilitation run progressively.
infrastructure: Haul roads, sediment ponds and clean-water diversions built before mining; sizing station relocated every 5–10 years.

routine.task: Haul-road grading and watering; spillage clean-up.
Windrow, edge-bund and ramp inspection and repair.
Floor and face pickup by machine GPS; pit water pumped to the sediment pond.

periodic.task: Formal survey weekly; ore/floor reconciliation against the grade-control model monthly.
Clean diversion drains and desilt sediment ponds.
periodic.interval: before the wet season and after major storms

overhaul.task: Relocation of the sizing station and road network as the mine moves.

symptoms: Low available Al₂O₃ or high reactive SiO₂ at the refinery
remedies: GPS bucket guidance, grade-control drilling, blending on the ROM pad

symptoms: Lower ore tonnes than the GC model
Bauxite left on the pit floor
causes: Stopping above the true ore/clay contact
remedies: GPS bucket guidance to the GC floor; floor pickup and reconciliation

items.problem: Wet-season sticky ore and poor trafficability
symptoms: Hopper bridging, truck carry-back, rutted ramps
remedies: Wet-weather dig plan from drier faces and the ROM-pad buffer; drainage; road-closure triggers
Maintain ponds and drains; stabilise disturbed ground quickly
Direct-return topsoil, deep ripping on the contour, seeding at the right season

safety: Heavy/light vehicle separation; light vehicles carry a buggy whip and flag, and give way to haul trucks
Windrows ≥ half the largest tyre height on every open edge, ramp and tip head
Face and crest: stay back from the crest; never work or park at the toe of a face being dug; keep out of the excavator swing radius
Blasting: exclusion zone set by the blast plan (commonly ≥ 500 m for people), guarding, sirens, all-clear; misfire procedure
Pre-start and shift road inspection; spillage removed (tyre cuts and loss of control)
Dust: water carts, pressurised cabs, respiratory protection where needed
Fatigue management and FMS proximity / collision-avoidance alarms
Phytophthora (dieback) hygiene: clean-on-entry and washdown between forest and mined areas where it is present
Sumps and ponds: fenced and signed, life rings, no lone work near water
Lightning / storm alert: stop work on exposed benches, decks and ramps and clear charged patterns
Wet roads: reduced speed limits; never over-water ramps and intersections
Brake test before descending; escape lanes or arrester berms on long downgrades
Traffic management plan: heavy vehicles have right of way, radio call-up before entering haul roads, keep-left one-way loops
Hopper: tip only on green, square to the wheel stop; ROM fingers and dumps: tip short and let the dozer push

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Mine — Area Overview (mining sequence).
Haul-road grading and watering; spillage clean-up.
Windrow, edge-bund and ramp inspection and repair.
Floor and face pickup by machine GPS; pit water pumped to the sediment pond.
Formal survey weekly; ore/floor reconciliation against the grade-control model monthly.
Clean diversion drains and desilt sediment ponds.
Relocation of the sizing station and road network as the mine moves.
Watch for ore dilution: low available Al₂O₃ or high reactive SiO₂ at the refinery. Common cause: digging past the ore/clay boundary.
Watch for ore loss: lower ore tonnes than the GC model. Common cause: stopping above the true ore/clay contact.
Watch for wet-season sticky ore and poor trafficability: hopper bridging, truck carry-back, rutted ramps. Common cause: mining clay-rich ore when wet.
Record road, windrow, pond and rehabilitation inspections so trends can be compared.

questions.question: Which layer is drilled and blasted?
questions.explanation: The cemented ferricrete cap is too hard to dig economically; the ore below is usually free-digging or ripped.

questions.question: Why is topsoil handled separately?
options: It is waste with no value
It contains the seed bank needed for rehabilitation
questions.explanation: Topsoil returned quickly gives the best regrowth.

questions.question: Where does mining stop at the bottom?
options: At the kaolinitic clay floor defined by grade control
questions.explanation: The clay below the ore is high in reactive silica.

questions.question: What is progressive rehabilitation?
options: Restoring mined pits continuously as mining moves on
questions.explanation: Pits are rehabilitated within a few years of mining.

questions.question: What two grade numbers matter most for the refinery?
questions.explanation: Available alumina makes product; reactive silica costs caustic and alumina.

questions.question: How high must a windrow on an open road edge be?
options: At least half the tyre height of the largest vehicle
As high as the truck cab
Windrows are only needed on curves
questions.explanation: A windrow of ≥ ½ tyre height (~1.4 m for 90 t trucks) gives the driver a tactile warning and helps stop a truck drifting over the edge; it is not a crash barrier.

questions.question: Which way does the mining face move in this model?
options: To the left, toward the rehabilitated land
To the right, into the forest; rehabilitation follows on the left
questions.explanation: Reading right to left shows one block through time; the face itself advances into the unmined ground.

controls: Fleet-management system assigns trucks; grade-control polygons in machine guidance; dispatch from the mine control room
start_up: Shift handover and pre-start meeting (blast notices, road closures, grade plan)
Machine pre-start inspections and radio check-in
Road and ramp inspection: windrows, drainage, spillage, wet-weather condition before the fleet is released
Confirm GC polygons and grade-bin destinations are loaded in GPS guidance and the FMS
normal: Mine to the plan and the grade bins; keep roads in good condition; progressive rehabilitation behind mining
shut_down: Park up in the designated park-up area, buckets and blades grounded
Blast-time clearance: all equipment and people outside the exclusion zone, guards posted, all-clear before re-entry
Wet-weather shutdown: close ramps and roads when traction or the rain trigger is exceeded
alarms_interlocks: Lightning alert: stop explosives charging and clear blast areas per the site lightning plan (typically lightning within ~10–16 km)
tips: Blend at the face and on the ROM pad — the refinery wants a steady available-alumina and reactive-silica feed
